headline: Highest risk is TREK’s default access to sensitive travel data and secrets; the pair otherwise has limited direct injection/conflict pathways because awesome-prompts is non-runnable and networkless.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is content-writing with no I/O surfaces and network egress none, so it cannot directly inject TREK. TREK does use MCP and browser/network tools, so if a user manually copies prompt content from awesome-prompts into TREK, prompt injection becomes possible, but that bridge is manual and not default.
conditions: IF the operator copies prompt text from awesome-prompts into TREK inputs
IF TREK treats copied text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep awesome-prompts and TREK in separate workspaces
Require a human review step before pasting prompt content into TREK
Disable or restrict MCP tools in TREK for untrusted text flows
Mark copied prompt libraries as untrusted content
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported prompt text

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts touches no data classes and has no network egress, so it is not a leakage source. TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, and it has allowlisted egress plus files/logs; if both share a workspace or TREK ingests copied content, sensitive travel data can leak through TREK’s outputs or logs.
conditions: IF TREK is given access to the same workspace as user documents
IF TREK logs or uploads files containing reservations, API keys, or MFA secrets
mitigations: Store TREK data in a separate directory with tight permissions
Remove secrets from uploads before using TREK
Review treks logs for sensitive fields and rotate exposed secrets
Limit TREK egress allowlist to required APIs only
requires-engineering: add redaction before logging or upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts has no write surfaces, concurrency model, or network egress, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. TREK supports multiple real-time collaborative instances and writes to ./data/travel.db, ./uploads/, and logs, so conflict is possible within TREK itself, but the pairwise overlap with awesome-prompts is minimal and read-only.
conditions: IF TREK instances share the same ./data/travel.db or ./uploads/ directory
IF multiple operators edit TREK state concurrently without locking
mitigations: Run each TREK instance in its own data directory
Avoid concurrent writes to the same travel.db
Use file locking or a single-writer pattern
Separate uploads per session
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts can supply prompt templates or instructions, and TREK is a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in, so TREK may treat imported prompt content as authoritative. Because TREK also acts on travel plans, reservations, and documents, a bad prompt from awesome-prompts can cascade into incorrect downstream actions unless TREK verifies inputs.
conditions: IF TREK uses imported prompt text as planning instructions
IF TREK forwards AI-generated travel recommendations into reservations or documents without verification
mitigations: Require confirmation before booking or editing reservations
Separate prompt templates from operational instructions
Add a verification step for AI-generated travel facts
Show source citations before acting on recommendations
requires-engineering: enforce policy checks before downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt repository with no touched data classes, while TREK handles travel plans, journal entries, reservations, user accounts, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. TREK’s logs and uploads create retention and residency exposure risks for those data classes; the pair is not a direct residency mismatch, but TREK’s handling of sensitive account data makes compliance controls necessary.
conditions: IF TREK stores personal travel records or secrets in ./data/logs/trek.log or ./uploads/
IF the deployment lacks a documented retention and deletion policy for TREK data
mitigations: Document retention periods for TREK logs and uploads
Restrict access to travel.db and uploads
Delete stale logs on a schedule
Separate secrets from general travel records
requires-engineering: implement subject-rights export and deletion workflows
